To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effluent tax rate should be set greater than the marginal cost of pollution if the externality between polluters is positive and that the effluent levy should be set less than the marginal cost if the externality is negative.

(i) the second-best tax rate is greater than the marginal external cost of pollution if the external cost is sufficiently high and the number of firms sufficiently large, and (ii) the second-best effluent tax rate is equal to the marginal external cost if the marginal social cost is less than or equal to the marginal private cost of pollution.
the second-best effluent tax is higher than the marginal social costs of pollution if and/or only if the marginal change of the equilibrium emission level with respect to the tax rate is negative.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a model of oligopolistic firms with externalities.
the design of corrective tax policy in a duopoly market with inter-firm externalities.
the optimal design of corrective taxes in a Cournot oligopoly with inter-firm externalities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the second-best tax is greater than the marginal cost of abatement if and only if there is a positive externality between the output and emission of the polluting firm.
the tax rate on a polluter should be set equal to its marginal social cost of emissions if and only if the tax rate is not too low to cause a decrease in the equilibrium emission level.
the second-best effluent tax rate is the sum of the marginal social costs of pollution and the negative externalities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the tax rate on a polluting firm depends not only on the marginal social cost, but also on the effects of the tax on the equilibrium emission level and the equilibrium output of other polluting firms.
the tax rate is determined not by the marginal social cost but by the marginal social damage, which is the sum of the marginal social cost and the marginal external damage.
the tax rate on a firm is determined by the marginal social cost, the marginal social benefits, and the inter-firm externalities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when the externalities between pollutors are substantial and/or when the number of pollutors is large, the optimal tax rate can be greater than the social marginal cost of pollution.
, when the externalities are significant, the tax rate can be higher than the marginal social costs of pollution.
the design of effluent levies is a complicated problem, and that the second-best tax rate should not be taken for granted.
